reason: Start by building the peripheral nerve route needed to carry sensory information inward and motor signals outward.
expectation: Schwann cells will wrap portions of the nerve fibres, likely forming peripheral myelin; how the routes connect remains to be seen.

alternatives.reason: Building the spinal cord also supports the routes, but I prefer to start at the periphery.

effect: The peripheral nerve is myelinated, with spikes renewed at gaps; I can now build a central connection.
reaction: The inset clarifies how the insulating wraps relate to signal propagation.
reason: Build the spinal cord as the next link from the peripheral nerve toward the brain.
expectation: The grey matter and longitudinal tracts will form a spinal cord cutaway, though the nerve connection may require another step.

alternatives.reason: The brain is also needed, but the spinal cord lies along the sensory route from the periphery.

effect: The grey matter and tracts now form a spinal cord, ready to connect to the peripheral nerve.
reaction: The cutaway makes their relative positions clear.
reason: Connect the peripheral nerve to the spinal cord to continue the sensory and motor routes.
expectation: The nerve will connect to the cord, showing routes into and out of it; the brain connection will still be needed.

alternatives.reason: The brain is also needed, but I want to complete the peripheral-to-spinal link first.

effect: The peripheral routes now connect to the cord, separating sensory entry from motor exit and leaving local circuits between them.
reaction: The shared nerve and separated cord routes are a useful distinction.
reason: Build the brain next so the sensory route can reach its destination.
expectation: The grey and white matter will form a brain model that can later connect to the spinal cord.

reason: Connect the brain and spinal cord to complete the central route before tracing sensory input.
expectation: The brain and cord will form a connected central pathway, with sensory and motor routes available to trace.

effect: The brain, spinal cord and peripheral nerves are connected, so I can now trace an input through the system.
reaction: The connected model makes the different routes easier to place, though their details remain to be traced.
reason: Trace pain input toward the brain, addressing the sensory goal and potentially setting up a spinal response.
expectation: I expect the pain signal to travel inward through peripheral and spinal pathways, possibly reaching the brain; the exact route is uncertain.

The cortical motor route is an option, but I want to trace sensation first.

effect: Pain input produced a coordinated spinal motor output, completing the motor goal without yet tracing sensation to the brain.
reaction: I was surprised that the pain combination led directly to a spinal response rather than an ascending sensory trace.
reason: Trace touch through the nervous system to address the remaining sensory goal.
expectation: I expect the touch signal to travel toward the brain, though the specific pathway is uncertain.

alternatives.reason: The cortical motor route is interesting, but the motor goal is already complete.

effect: Touch input traced a sensory route through the cord, brainstem and thalamus to the cortex, completing the remaining goal.
reaction: The labelled thalamic relay gives the long route a useful landmark, though the pathway remains broad.

mostWorthwhile.text: Connecting the peripheral nerve to the cord made the shared nerve and the separation of sensory entry from motor exit clear. It also set up the contrast between local spinal circuits and longer routes.

leastWorthwhile.text: Assembling the brain and cord was fairly predictable, and the resulting pathway descriptions stayed broad. The planned pictures show their arrangement but give limited detail about the connections.

surprise.text: I expected pain input might trace sensation toward the brain, but it instead produced a coordinated spinal motor response without waiting for conscious perception.

arbitrary.text: The pain input's direct jump to motor output was not arbitrary once explained, but its selection did not make that result obvious beforehand. No other action felt clearly purposeless.

continue.text: Yes, tentatively: the contrast between spinal and cortical routes is interesting, and I would like to see the cortical motor route explored. The assembly steps themselves were less compelling.
